forces.title: Higher interest rates dampening Belgian mortgage activity.
forces.description: Persistent high long-term interest rates, influenced by ongoing geopolitical conflict in the Middle East, are expected to keep financing conditions restrictive in Belgium. This leads to weaker mortgage production, with new mortgages in H1 2026 down 10% year-on-year. For Fixed Income, Debt & IBC, this creates a headwind for the supply of new mortgage debt and, consequently, for mortgage-backed securitisation volumes. It also implies increased debt service costs for existing variable-rate mortgages, potentially affecting credit quality.
forces.source_title: Second-quarter resilience masks a more challenging outlook for Belgian housing

forces.title: Low Norwegian construction activity dampens related debt demand.
forces.description: Norges Bank contacts report persistently low construction activity in Norway, with few new residential and commercial projects. The expected upturn in residential construction is continually delayed, and municipal construction projects are decreasing. This low activity leads to dampened order volumes for related services like architects and technical consultants. For the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, this translates to reduced demand for construction financing, project debt, and potentially fewer municipal bond issuances for public works.
forces.source_title: Regional Network report 3/2026: Minor changes in growth prospects

forces.title: Weak profitability and fierce competition in Norwegian construction.
forces.description: Norges Bank's Regional Network reports that profitability in the Norwegian construction sector remains weak, characterized by fierce competition for contracts. Despite some contacts noting slightly improved margins from higher activity or completion of unprofitable fixed-price contracts, the overall sector faces significant pressure. This weak profitability increases the risk of corporate defaults and insolvencies within the construction industry, posing a credit risk for lenders and investors in corporate debt instruments tied to this sector.
forces.source_title: Regional Network report 3/2026: Minor changes in growth prospects

forces.title: High insolvency risk for Irish hospitality sector in 2026.
forces.description: Allianz Ireland forecasts a continued high proportion of insolvencies in the Irish hospitality sector (pubs and restaurants) for the remainder of 2026. This is driven by profitability tightening due to rising fuel prices, increased processing and transport costs, and broader macroeconomic pressures. For the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, this implies an elevated risk of defaults on corporate debt issued by hospitality businesses and an increased volume of insolvency resolution cases, impacting credit quality and recovery rates for lenders and investors.
forces.source_title: July 2026 Ireland Sector Snippets

forces.title: Lower interest rates support Irish automotive retail financing.
forces.description: Ireland's automotive retail sector is experiencing buoyant market trends, supported significantly by lower interest rates and competitive incentives for new and used cars. This positive financing environment is driving increased new car registrations, with electrified vehicles now accounting for over 56% of the market. For the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, lower interest rates provide a tailwind for consumer auto lending and potentially auto asset-backed securitisation, by making debt more affordable for consumers and stimulating demand for vehicle financing.
forces.source_title: July 2026 Ireland Sector Snippets

forces.title: Rising insolvencies in Irish retail sector amidst challenging environment.
forces.description: Ireland's retail sector is struggling with a challenging trading environment, marked by declining real sales volumes and uneven consumer spending due to cost-of-living pressures. Subsectors like clothing, footwear & textiles, fuel, department stores, and electrical goods have seen notable declines. Allianz Ireland highlights increasing insolvency levels across parts of the sector, which warrants close attention. This presents a key risk for Fixed Income, Debt & IBC, indicating potential defaults on corporate debt for retail businesses and a higher demand for insolvency resolution services.
forces.source_title: July 2026 Ireland Sector Snippets

forces.title: Elevated interest rates challenge Irish aircraft leasing sector.
forces.description: Ireland's transport equipment sector, dominated by aircraft leasing, is performing well due to global aviation recovery. However, the sector faces significant challenges from elevated interest rates, which increase financing costs for lessors acquiring and managing their fleet portfolios. Given the capital-intensive nature of aircraft leasing and its reliance on debt financing, higher interest rates serve as a direct headwind to corporate debt within this sector, potentially impacting profitability and expansion plans, despite strong market demand for aircraft.
forces.source_title: July 2026 Ireland Sector Snippets

forces.title: Declining farm income increases credit risk for Irish agricultural debt.
forces.description: The Irish agricultural sector, particularly tillage farms, faces declining incomes in 2026. Teagasc forecasts a decrease in market-based output value for cereals due to lower production volume and unchanged cereal prices compared to 2025. Simultaneously, direct costs for tillage farms are expected to rise by 5%, primarily from higher fertilizer and fuel prices. This squeeze on margins leads to lower average farm incomes, increasing the credit risk associated with agricultural loans and corporate bonds issued by agri-businesses, and potentially leading to higher defaults or demand for debt restructuring.
forces.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

forces.title: Rising food prices and overheads strain Irish grocery sector's debt capacity.
forces.description: The Irish grocery and convenience sector faces persistent food price increases in 2026, driven by higher global commodity prices (wheat, sugar, cocoa), increased overheads for retailers and suppliers (personnel, energy, insurance), rising farm-gate prices, and global trade uncertainty exacerbated by the Middle East conflict. These factors lead to an already stretched cost base and focus on margin development/preservation. For Fixed Income, Debt & IBC, this constitutes a headwind by increasing financial pressure on grocery retailers and their suppliers, potentially affecting their ability to service existing corporate debt and limiting their capacity for new financing.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Retail Convenience H1 2026 Insights and H2 2026 Outlook July 2026

forces.title: Mobilizing €12 trillion European household savings towards capital markets.
forces.description: Europe faces a significant opportunity to mobilize approximately €12 trillion in liquid assets held by European households in cash and deposits towards capital markets. This represents a substantial, largely untapped pool of capital that could be directed into various financial instruments, including fixed income products. Shifting these savings away from low-return vehicles towards investments would deepen European capital markets, providing a tailwind for bond issuances and overall debt market activity by increasing liquidity and demand from individual investors.
forces.source_title: Cash, Capital, and Culture: Mobilizing Household Savings to Close the European Investment Gap

forces.title: Deep-seated risk aversion and low financial literacy among European households.
forces.description: A BCG digital forum revealed that financial caution is deeply rooted among European households, with roughly two-thirds unwilling to take risks with savings. Less than 30% participate in capital markets, and over 50% prefer low-return vehicles like cash and deposits. This widespread risk aversion, coupled with limited financial literacy, acts as a significant structural headwind for the development and growth of European capital markets, including fixed income. It limits the potential retail investor base for bonds and other debt instruments.
forces.source_title: Cash, Capital, and Culture: Mobilizing Household Savings to Close the European Investment Gap

forces.title: Increasing financial knowledge to boost European capital market participation.
forces.description: BCG's digital forum suggests that providing simple, trustworthy information and increasing financial knowledge among European households could significantly shift their reserved attitude toward capital markets. This educational intervention, particularly when applied to sensitive areas like pensions, has shown to make Europeans more open to market-based risk. This acts as a potential upside driver for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector by fostering greater retail investor engagement, increasing demand for various debt instruments, and thereby deepening the overall capital markets.
forces.source_title: Cash, Capital, and Culture: Mobilizing Household Savings to Close the European Investment Gap

forces.title: Prospects of higher interest rates reduce customer and investment appetite in Norway.
forces.description: Norges Bank's Regional Network contacts report that customers are becoming more hesitant due to the prospects of higher interest rates and stronger cost growth. This is leading to halted or postponed projects and orders across several Norwegian sectors, including technology, strategic advisory services, marketing, and real estate development. For the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, this represents a cyclical headwind as higher borrowing costs reduce demand for new corporate debt, potentially increase the cost of capital for businesses, and impact the overall volume of new bond issuances.
forces.source_title: Regional Network report 2/2026: Recruitment difficulties have eased somewhat

forces.title: Higher interest rates postpone Norwegian residential construction recovery.
forces.description: The Norwegian construction sector continues to experience dampened growth, specifically in new residential builds. Norges Bank's contacts report that the anticipated pickup in residential construction is persistently postponed, primarily attributed to higher interest rates and expectations of further increases in building costs. For the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, this serves as a headwind by reducing demand for new construction financing and project debt, as developers delay projects due to increased borrowing costs, thus limiting new corporate debt issuance related to real estate development.
forces.source_title: Regional Network report 2/2026: Recruitment difficulties have eased somewhat

forces.title: Private credit diversifies beyond direct lending with asset-backed finance.
forces.description: The private credit market is undergoing a structural shift as strategies beyond traditional direct lending, particularly asset-backed finance (ABF) and credit secondaries, are scaling rapidly. This diversification is driven by capital seeking new avenues away from a compressed core market. ABF, in particular, is expanding into infrastructure, residential mortgages, and commercial real estate, with its addressable market in the US alone potentially exceeding $30 trillion. This trend represents a structural tailwind for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector by expanding the types of debt products available for private investment and enhancing market depth.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Wealth and insurance capital increasingly fund private credit.
forces.description: Fundraising for private credit is experiencing a structural evolution, with wealth and insurance capital accounting for a rising share of inflows across diverse vehicles like BDCs, evergreen funds, and insurance mandates. Insurers are particularly drawn to private credit's predictable, yield-generating cash flows, while offering stable, long-duration capital. This shift reshapes the deployment cadence and liability profile of the asset class, providing a robust and stable funding base for various corporate and structured debt products within the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Increasing defaults and liquidity concerns challenge leveraged private credit.
forces.description: The private credit market faces mounting challenges, including a series of defaults and losses in leveraged credit that have garnered significant attention. Additionally, liquidity concerns have emerged for many semi-liquid private credit vehicles, evidenced by BDC share prices trading below net asset value and a sharp increase in redemption activity. This heightened scrutiny on credit quality and managers' due diligence poses a key risk for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, signaling potential underperformance and increased volatility in certain segments of corporate debt.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Intensifying competition in private credit from banks and BSL market.
forces.description: Competition in the private credit market is intensifying significantly, not only from within the sector due to high dry powder but also from traditional banks and the broadly syndicated loan (BSL) market. Banks are increasingly acting as direct principals for private-credit-style loans, competing on speed and execution. Furthermore, refinancing flows between BSL and direct lending markets are approaching parity, marking a clear break from prior one-directional flows. This structural shift creates a more competitive environment for direct lending within Fixed Income, Debt & IBC, potentially pressuring spreads and terms.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Private credit spread compression and declining new-issue yields.
forces.description: Intensified competition in the private credit market has led to pricing and terms shifting in favor of borrowers. Global new-issue, direct loan median spreads have significantly compressed, falling from 716 basis points in March 2023 to 544 basis points by year-end 2025. Concurrently, upfront fee economics have declined, and all-in new-issue yields for direct loans decreased to approximately 9.3% in 2025 from 10.5% in 2024. This trend creates a headwind for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector by reducing potential returns for investors in private credit and corporate debt.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Borrower-friendly terms and covenant-lite deals increase private credit risk.
forces.description: Loan documentation in the private credit market is becoming increasingly borrower-friendly, particularly in the upper-middle market where it competes with syndicated financing. Covenant-lite transactions have surged to 21% of direct lending deals in 2025, a substantial increase from 4% in 2023. This trend, coupled with leverage ratios on new-issue transactions remaining elevated (averaging 4.9x EBITDA in 2025), signifies an increase in credit risk. For Fixed Income, Debt & IBC, these weaker underwriting standards could lead to higher default rates and lower recovery rates in future downturns for corporate debt investors.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Surge in distressed debt fundraising signals anticipated opportunities.
forces.description: Fundraising for private credit strategies diversified in 2025, with strategies outside direct lending growing by 22% year-over-year. Distressed debt led this growth, surging nearly 180%, anchored by Oaktree Capital Management's $16 billion fund. This significant increase signals that investors anticipate attractive distressed opportunities to arise in 2026, driven by potential market dislocations or credit quality concerns. For the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, this represents an upside driver for specialized debt funds focused on restructuring and recovery.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Surge in redemptions challenges liquidity of semi-liquid private credit.
forces.description: Semi-liquid private credit vehicles, including BDCs and evergreen funds, experienced a sharp increase in redemption activity in late 2025, with Q4 redemptions nearly tripling over the prior quarter to average 4.5% of NAV. This accelerated into Q1 2026, posing a significant test for the asset class. This liquidity challenge, driven by concerns over credit quality and market sentiment, presents a key risk for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, particularly for managers heavily reliant on the wealth channel, potentially forcing asset sales or limiting new capital deployment.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Evergreen and open-end private credit AUM sees robust growth.
forces.description: Capital formation in private credit is increasingly occurring outside traditional closed-end structures. Evergreen and open-end private credit Assets Under Management (AUM) grew by approximately 27% year-over-year in 2025, encompassing growth in Business Development Companies (BDCs), interval funds, and tender offer vehicles. This structural shift towards continuous capital raising mechanisms supports a more consistent deployment of capital into various debt instruments. It represents a significant development for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector by providing more flexible and accessible investment vehicles for private debt.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Insurers increasingly allocate to private credit, especially investment-grade and ABF.
forces.description: The convergence of insurance and private credit continues, with insurers increasingly viewing private credit as a source of predictable, yield-generating cash flows and a destination for stable, long-duration capital. A 2025 survey found 58% of insurance CIOs planning to increase private credit allocations, with notable interest in investment-grade private credit (40%) and asset-backed finance (36%). This preference positions insurers as key catalysts for the expansion of private credit beyond leveraged lending, representing a significant tailwind for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector by providing deep institutional demand for diverse debt products.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Strong institutional LP conviction fuels private credit allocation growth.
forces.description: Institutional Limited Partners (LPs) are showing firm and growing conviction in private credit, with 40% planning to increase allocations over the next 12 months, a rise from 38% in the prior year. This sustained positive sentiment stems from private credit's attractive features, including its senior position in the capital structure, predictable income profile, and narrow return dispersion. This strong institutional demand acts as a significant tailwind for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, ensuring a robust and consistent flow of capital into corporate debt and other private credit instruments.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Wealth channel momentum for private credit stalls amidst redemption spike.
forces.description: While institutional conviction in private credit remains strong, the wealth channel exhibits a murkier picture. Although net inflows were positive in 2025, momentum has stalled, and fundraising in 2026 suggests potential reversal due to a spike in redemption requests. Private credit capital in semi-liquid structures from the wealth channel represents a significant portion of AUM for several large managers, making its durability a central question for the asset class. This poses a key risk for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, particularly regarding liquidity management for affected funds.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

forces.title: Infrastructure credit fuels asset-backed finance growth due to AI buildout.
forces.description: Infrastructure credit is a rapidly expanding segment within asset-backed finance (ABF), driven by the immense capital requirements for AI buildout projects such as data centers, fiber networks, and power generation. This need is projected to drive $106 trillion in infrastructure investment over the next 14 years. This surge in demand for infrastructure financing creates a significant upside driver for the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, particularly for ABF and corporate debt related to digital and energy infrastructure development.
forces.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

viewpoints.title: Belgian housing resilience to fade amid weaker mortgage lending and higher rates.
viewpoints.description: The Belgian housing market showed unexpected resilience in Q2 2026 with modest price increases and transaction recovery. However, this momentum is likely unsustainable due to weakening mortgage production and persistently high interest rates, driven by geopolitical tensions. Mortgage lending figures were down 10% year-on-year for the first eight months of 2026. While energy-efficient homes might maintain demand due to rising energy costs, the overall market is forecast to cool, with nominal median house prices increasing by only 2.5% in 2026 and 2.0% in 2027. This suggests a cautious outlook for new mortgage issuance, which in turn impacts potential for securitisation of residential mortgage debt.
viewpoints.source_title: Second-quarter resilience masks a more challenging outlook for Belgian housing

viewpoints.title: Irish construction debt stable despite supply chain reliance on short-term credit.
viewpoints.description: Allianz Ireland observes continued strengthening in Irish construction activity, characterized by sustained new order inflows and broad-based recovery. The sector's debt levels are currently low, and cash positions are healthy, contributing to low insolvency rates. However, a cautious note is struck regarding parts of the supply chain, which remain reliant on overdrafts, invoice discounting, and trade credit. This implies a generally stable, albeit watchful, outlook for corporate debt in the core construction sector, with pockets of risk in its extended supply chain that rely on short-term financing.

viewpoints.title: Irish metals sector shows resilience despite cost pressures and softer prices.
viewpoints.description: The Irish metals sector is supported by its links to construction, engineering, manufacturing, and agri-business. Despite facing headwinds such as softer global metal prices, persistent raw material and labor cost pressures, and trade policy uncertainty, the sector demonstrates resilience with generally stable trading conditions. Liquidity remains favorable among major steel stockholders, and insolvency levels are low. This suggests that the corporate debt related to the Irish metals sector is currently stable, but continuous monitoring of input costs and pricing power is essential to mitigate potential credit risks.

viewpoints.title: Irish tillage farm incomes forecast to decrease in 2026 due to costs and lower output.
viewpoints.description: Teagasc forecasts a decrease in Irish tillage farm incomes for 2026, with average farm income expected to remain below €45,000, and below €40,000 for specialist tillage farms. This negative outlook is driven by a forecast decrease in output value due to lower cereal production volumes (down approximately 10%) and stagnant cereal prices in 2026 relative to 2025. Concurrently, direct costs on tillage farms are expected to rise by about 5% compared to 2025, primarily due to increases in fertilizer and fuel prices. This situation creates a cautious-negative outlook for the credit quality of agricultural debt in Ireland.
viewpoints.source_title: Mid-Year Situation and Outlook for Irish Agriculture July 2026

viewpoints.title: Private credit matures with increasing complexity and competitive pressures.
viewpoints.description: McKinsey views the private credit asset class as maturing, transitioning from a simpler leveraged corporate lending sector to a complex ecosystem with diverse strategies and capital pools. The industry is navigating an increasingly challenging performance environment marked by cyclical and structural risks, requiring precision over pace in capital deployment. While dealmaking sustained near-record volumes in 2025, it involved fewer but larger deals amid intensifying competition and tightening spreads. This indicates a cautious but evolving outlook for private credit, emphasizing the need for strategic adaptation to new market dynamics.
viewpoints.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

viewpoints.title: Private credit performance held steady in 2025 despite market uncertainties.
viewpoints.description: McKinsey reports that private credit performance remained largely consistent with historical levels in 2025, with a pooled net Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of 8.5%, up from 7.0% in 2024. This performance occurred despite declining new-issue yields and concerns over potential defaults. The asset class maintained a narrow return dispersion compared to other private market asset classes, indicating relative stability. This suggests a resilient, albeit scrutinized, performance for private credit within the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, affirming its appeal to institutional investors seeking predictable income.
viewpoints.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

viewpoints.title: Institutional investors show firm conviction in private credit despite headwinds.
viewpoints.description: Institutional limited partners maintain strong conviction in private credit, with 40% planning to increase allocations in the next 12 months, surpassing planned increases for private equity or real estate. This positive sentiment is driven by private credit's senior position in the capital structure, predictable income profile, and narrow return dispersion. While credit quality indicators generally remain within historical ranges (e.g., improved interest coverage), the outlook for the wealth channel is murkier due to stalled momentum and increasing redemption requests. Overall, this indicates sustained institutional demand supporting the private debt market.
viewpoints.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

demand_drivers.description: Encouraging European households to shift from cash/deposit holdings to market investments.

new_opportunities.description: Mobilizing €12 trillion in household savings could significantly increase demand and liquidity for bond markets and other debt instruments from retail investors across Europe, diversifying the investor base.
new_opportunities.opportunity: Increased Retail Participation in Fixed Income

market_sizing.methodology: BCG analysis suggests a potential pool of €12 trillion in liquid assets (cash and deposits) held by European households that could be mobilized towards capital markets. This represents an opportunity to deepen capital markets by attracting individual investor funds into investments, including fixed income products, which are currently held in low-return vehicles.
market_sizing.source_title: Cash, Capital, and Culture: Mobilizing Household Savings to Close the European Investment Gap

demand_drivers.description: Large corporations seek to optimize capital structure through direct lending.

market_sizing.methodology: The €6.5 billion unitranche refinancing for Norwegian online classifieds group, Adevinta, represents the largest direct lending deal on record in 2025. This deal highlights the ongoing up-market migration of direct lending strategies, with increasing deal sizes becoming a feature of the market. This figure contributes to the understanding of the scale of corporate debt activity and direct lending within the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector in Europe.
market_sizing.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

market_sizing.methodology: Global closed-end private credit fundraising declined 16% year-over-year in 2025, reaching approximately $165 billion. This figure excludes secondaries and funds of funds. Direct lending funds, a significant component, saw a 28% decline in fundraising. This indicates a moderation in capital raising for traditional private credit vehicles, even as other forms of capital formation (e.g., evergreen funds, insurance mandates) gain prominence. This provides a sizing for a key segment of corporate debt within Fixed Income, Debt & IBC.
market_sizing.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

demand_drivers.driver: Investor demand for scaled private credit managers
demand_drivers.description: Large institutional investors prefer allocating capital to established managers with broad product offerings and diversified holds.

market_sizing.methodology: Ares Management's €17.1 billion fundraising for its sixth flagship European fund in 2025 represents the largest closed-end private credit vehicle ever based on LP commitments. This significant figure underscores the continued ability of scaled managers to attract substantial capital for corporate debt strategies within the European Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, despite a broader moderation in closed-end fundraising volumes.
market_sizing.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

demand_drivers.driver: Investor demand for diversified private credit strategies
demand_drivers.description: Capital seeks opportunities beyond traditional direct lending.

market_sizing.methodology: Closed-end funds focused on Asset-Backed Finance (ABF) opportunities globally raised approximately $27.1 billion in 2025, accounting for 16.4% of all closed-end private credit fundraising. This marks a notable increase from 10.6% market share in 2024. While this figure primarily represents closed-end funds, the managed assets in the broader private ABF market are larger due to insurance-linked and other capital not captured in traditional fundraising. This provides a sizing for the securitisation segment within Fixed Income, Debt & IBC.
market_sizing.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

demand_drivers.driver: Demand for private credit liquidity solutions
demand_drivers.description: Maturing private credit funds and semi-liquid vehicles drive the need for secondary market transactions.

new_opportunities.description: The growth of private credit secondaries offers price discovery and liquidity to an asset class traditionally held to maturity, benefiting investors and fund managers.

market_sizing.methodology: Private credit secondaries deal volumes nearly doubled from 2024 to reach $20 billion globally in 2025. GP-led volume tripled to $12 billion (60% of total), while LP-led volume grew by 16% to $8 billion. This rapid growth, driven by demand for liquidity solutions in a maturing asset class, highlights a significant and expanding segment within the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector. Dedicated secondaries buyers also raised substantial capital, indicating strong market interest and further growth potential.
market_sizing.source_title: Private credit in 2025: A maturing industry navigates change

demand_drivers.driver: Demand for novel digital asset structures
demand_drivers.description: Increasing interest in blockchain technology for representing real-world assets.

new_opportunities.description: Tokenization could enable new forms of corporate debt, securitisation, and InvIT/REIT debt, offering fractional ownership, improved liquidity, and enhanced transparency.

market_sizing.methodology: The global market capitalization for tokenized real-world assets reached approximately $30 billion in 2025. This emerging digital asset class, while currently modest in scale, has implications for future debt structures within the Fixed Income, Debt & IBC sector, potentially offering new ways to securitize and trade assets.
